output.impression: 1. Symmetric T1 hyperintensity of the globi pallidi without diffusion restriction, a pattern seen with chronic liver disease and manganese deposition. 2. Mild generalized volume loss. 3. No acute infarct, hemorrhage, extra-axial collection or mass lesion; no mammillary body or medial thalamic signal change; no mesial temporal signal abnormality.

alternatives: Levetiracetam is less than 10 percent hepatically metabolized and is primarily renally cleared; reduce the dose for a creatinine clearance below 50 mL/min. Lacosamide is an alternative with moderate hepatic dose reduction.
contraindications: Valproate in hepatic failure: directly hepatotoxic and raises ammonia by inhibiting the urea cycle; contraindicated here.
interactions: Benzodiazepines + Child-Pugh C cirrhosis: hepatic clearance is reduced and the half-life markedly prolonged, with accumulation and deepening of encephalopathy through GABA-A potentiation; a single diagnostic dose under EEG is acceptable, maintenance dosing is not.
Valproate + cirrhosis with hyperammonemia: additive hyperammonemia and hepatotoxicity; avoid.

Fosphenytoin + hypoalbuminemia (albumin 2.2 g/dL) and hepatic impairment: the free fraction rises, so total levels underestimate exposure and loading causes hypotension; if used, monitor free phenytoin.
Rifaximin + levetiracetam, lactulose or spironolactone: no clinically relevant interaction; rifaximin is minimally absorbed.
Propranolol + acute decompensation with a low mean arterial pressure and rising creatinine: reduces cardiac output and renal perfusion; hold during the acute episode.
Spironolactone and furosemide + acute kidney injury or hyponatremia: hold during the acute episode and resume once renal function and sodium have recovered.
output.proposed: Levetiracetam, lacosamide, valproate, fosphenytoin or a benzodiazepine with lactulose, rifaximin, propranolol, spironolactone and furosemide in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis

output.query: Hepatic encephalopathy: triphasic waves, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis and treatment targets

results.finding: Overt hepatic encephalopathy is treated by identifying and correcting the precipitant and by lactulose titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools per day, with rifaximin added as an adjunct to prevent recurrence; ammonia measurement neither establishes nor excludes the diagnosis and is not used to titrate therapy.

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is defined by an ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear count of 250 cells/mm3 or more and is treated empirically with a third-generation cephalosporin; intravenous albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 reduces renal failure and mortality in patients with a bilirubin above 4 mg/dL or creatinine above 1 mg/dL.
Non-selective beta blockers and diuretics are withheld during acute decompensation with hypotension or acute kidney injury and resumed once the patient is stable.

Generalized periodic discharges with triphasic morphology occur in metabolic encephalopathies and also in non-convulsive status epilepticus; morphology alone does not separate them, while reactivity, evolution and the response to an intravenous antiseizure medication inform the distinction.

Discharges at 2.5 Hz or less in a patient without known epileptic encephalopathy meet criteria for non-convulsive status epilepticus only with typical spatiotemporal evolution, subtle ictal clinical phenomena or clinical and electrographic improvement after an intravenous antiseizure medication.

output.summary: Overt hepatic encephalopathy is treated by correcting the precipitant and giving lactulose to 2 to 3 soft stools per day with rifaximin as an adjunct, and ammonia is not used to titrate therapy [Vilstrup_2014]. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is defined by 250 or more polymorphonuclear cells per mm3 and treated with a third-generation cephalosporin plus albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 [AASLD_ascites_2021], and beta blockers and diuretics are withheld during acute decompensation [EASL_decomp_2018]. Triphasic morphology does not by itself separate metabolic encephalopathy from non-convulsive status epilepticus; reactivity, evolution and the response to an intravenous antiseizure medication do [ACNS_2021; Salzburg_NCSE_2015].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Ammonia 186 umol/L; bilirubin 8.6 mg/dL, INR 3.2, albumin 2.2 g/dL and platelets 82 x10^9/L (Child-Pugh C); sodium 128, potassium 3.2, glucose 62 mg/dL, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL with BUN 42; WBC 12.4 x10^9/L
action_criteria.label: Emergency laboratory work-up: glucose, CBC, electrolytes, magnesium, renal and hepatic function, ammonia, coagulation
action_criteria.rationale: Glucose, electrolyte, renal and hepatic derangements are reversible causes of impaired consciousness and decide the ASM and its dose; ammonia and coagulation because the patient has decompensated cirrhosis, and the coagulation profile and platelet count decide whether an LP is safe [Brophy_2012; Vilstrup_2014].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Ascitic polymorphonuclear count 558 cells/mm3 (680 nucleated cells, 82 percent neutrophils), at or above the 250 cells/mm3 threshold: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; protein 0.9 g/dL with a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.6 g/dL; Gram stain negative
action_criteria.label: Diagnostic paracentesis: ascitic fluid cell count with differential, protein, Gram stain and culture in blood-culture bottles at the bedside
action_criteria.rationale: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is the commonest precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy and is often afebrile; only the ascitic polymorphonuclear count identifies it, and coagulopathy is not a contraindication to paracentesis [AASLD_ascites_2021].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Two sets drawn before antimicrobials, no growth to date; a negative culture does not exclude peritonitis
action_criteria.label: Two sets of blood cultures before the first antimicrobial dose
action_criteria.rationale: Bacteremia accompanies spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in a substantial minority of patients and would narrow the antibiotic; it is recommended rather than required because the paracentesis establishes the diagnosis and treatment does not wait for it [AASLD_ascites_2021].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No extra-axial collection, hemorrhage, mass or midline shift; mild generalized volume loss
action_criteria.label: Non-contrast head CT to exclude a subdural hematoma and other structural cause
action_criteria.rationale: A confused cirrhotic patient with INR 3.2 and platelets 82 x10^9/L can have an unwitnessed subdural hematoma, which would change management entirely [Brophy_2012].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Generalized periodic discharges with triphasic morphology at 1.5-2 Hz with anterior-to-posterior phase lag, attenuating with stimulation, plus intermittent left temporal 3-4 Hz rhythmic runs without evolution; no unequivocal electrographic seizure, both patterns on the ictal-interictal continuum
action_criteria.label: Continuous video-EEG to characterize the periodic pattern and look for electrographic seizures
action_criteria.rationale: Impaired consciousness with unexplained rhythmic limb movements needs EEG; triphasic morphology does not by itself separate metabolic encephalopathy from non-convulsive status epilepticus, so reactivity, evolution and the clinical correlate are what the recording must document [Brophy_2012; ACNS_2021].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Symmetric globus pallidus T1 hyperintensity without diffusion restriction (chronic liver disease); no acute infarct, hemorrhage or extra-axial collection; no mammillary body or medial thalamic signal change
action_criteria.label: MRI brain if the encephalopathy does not improve with treatment of the precipitant
action_criteria.rationale: MRI is recommended, not required: the precipitant is identified and the CT has excluded the dangerous structural cause, so MRI matters only if the encephalopathy persists, when it also addresses Wernicke encephalopathy and a missed lesion [Glauser_2016; Vilstrup_2014].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Valproate contraindicated (hepatotoxic, raises ammonia); benzodiazepines accumulate in Child-Pugh C and deepen encephalopathy, acceptable only as a single diagnostic dose; fosphenytoin free fraction rises with albumin 2.2 g/dL; levetiracetam is minimally hepatically metabolized and renally dosed; hold propranolol and the diuretics during the acute episode
action_criteria.label: Drug-interaction and hepatic-dosing check before any ASM, and review of the cirrhosis medications
action_criteria.rationale: Child-Pugh C cirrhosis with hyperammonemia, albumin 2.2 g/dL and a creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL makes valproate contraindicated, benzodiazepines hazardous as maintenance and fosphenytoin unpredictable, and the beta blocker and diuretics need review during the acute decompensation [Brophy_2012; EASL_decomp_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General cited evidence on lactulose and rifaximin targets, the peritonitis threshold with albumin, and the limits of triphasic morphology
action_criteria.label: Literature on hepatic encephalopathy, triphasic waves and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
action_criteria.rationale: Optional background on the treatment targets and on separating triphasic patterns from seizures; it is not a clinical step [Vilstrup_2014].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give valproate: it is hepatotoxic and raises ammonia in a patient already encephalopathic with cirrhosis.
Do not use maintenance benzodiazepines; a single diagnostic dose under EEG is acceptable, continued dosing deepens the encephalopathy.
Do not perform a lumbar puncture with an INR of 3.2 and platelets of 82 x10^9/L in the absence of fever, meningism or another indication.
Do not escalate to an anaesthetic infusion for a periodic pattern with no electrographic seizures and no response to a benzodiazepine trial.
required_recommendations: Treat spontaneous bacterial peritonitis empirically with IV cefotaxime 2 g every 8 hours (or ceftriaxone 2 g daily), adjusted later to the culture result [AASLD_ascites_2021].

Give IV albumin 1.5 g/kg within 6 hours and 1 g/kg on day 3: bilirubin 8.6 mg/dL and creatinine 1.6 mg/dL place him in the group in which albumin reduces renal failure and mortality [AASLD_ascites_2021].

Continue lactulose titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools per day (nasogastric or rectal if he cannot swallow safely) and continue rifaximin 550 mg twice daily; do not use ammonia levels to titrate therapy [Vilstrup_2014].
Hold propranolol, spironolactone and furosemide during this decompensation with a creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL, and resume once renal function and sodium recover [EASL_decomp_2018].

Give IV thiamine 200 to 500 mg before or with any glucose, and correct the glucose of 62 mg/dL and the potassium of 3.2 mEq/L; correct hyponatremia of 128 mEq/L slowly, by no more than 8 mmol/L in 24 hours, because alcohol-related liver disease and malnutrition make osmotic demyelination likely [Spasovski_2014; EFNS_Wernicke_2010].

Give a single IV lorazepam 2 mg diagnostic trial under continuous EEG to test the ictal-interictal pattern, and continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours; if the pattern and the examination improve, load IV levetiracetam 20 to 40 mg/kg adjusted for a creatinine clearance below 50 mL/min rather than continuing benzodiazepines [Brophy_2012; ESETT_2019].
Refer to hepatology and screen for transplant candidacy, and explain the prognosis of Child-Pugh C cirrhosis with peritonitis to the patient's wife [EASL_decomp_2018].

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

LP is not indicated: the patient is afebrile with an identified precipitant (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) and no meningism, and with an INR of 3.2 and platelets of 82 x10^9/L the puncture carries a real risk of spinal hematoma.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy from Child-Pugh C cirrhosis with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis precipitating acute decompensation; EEG triphasic waves mimicking non-convulsive status epilepticus

differential.diagnosis: Non-convulsive status epilepticus in a cirrhotic patient
differential.key_features: Triphasic morphology does not exclude it and the left temporal rhythmic runs lie on the ictal-interictal continuum; no evolution and the attenuation with stimulation argue against it, so a benzodiazepine trial under EEG is needed before it is dismissed
Former heavy drinker with poor intake, but no ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus or ataxia and no mammillary body or medial thalamic signal change on MRI; thiamine is given empirically regardless
INR 3.2 with platelets 82 x10^9/L makes it plausible, but the CT shows no extra-axial collection and the MRI no susceptibility signal loss

differential.diagnosis: Bacterial meningitis or another central nervous system infection
differential.key_features: Afebrile without meningism, a peritoneal source is identified, and the coagulopathy makes LP unsafe; blood cultures show no growth
No sedative on the medication list and the toxicology history is negative, but the diuretics contribute to the hyponatremia and the renal impairment
Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL with BUN 42 reflects a hepatorenal pattern rather than uremia at a level that causes encephalopathy

key_clinical_evidence: Generalized periodic discharges with triphasic morphology occur both in metabolic encephalopathy and in non-convulsive status epilepticus; morphology alone does not separate them, while reactivity to stimulation, absence of evolution and the response to an IV antiseizure medication do [ACNS_2021; Salzburg_NCSE_2015].

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is the commonest precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy, is frequently afebrile, and is diagnosed by an ascitic polymorphonuclear count of 250 cells/mm3 or more; coagulopathy does not contraindicate the paracentesis [AASLD_ascites_2021].
Albumin 1.5 g/kg on day 1 and 1 g/kg on day 3 reduces renal failure and mortality in peritonitis with bilirubin above 4 mg/dL or creatinine above 1 mg/dL [AASLD_ascites_2021].
Lactulose is titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools per day, with rifaximin as an adjunct; ammonia levels neither establish the diagnosis nor guide titration [Vilstrup_2014].

Levetiracetam is the antiseizure medication of choice in liver failure (under 10 percent hepatic metabolism, renally dosed); valproate is contraindicated and benzodiazepines accumulate in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Triphasic morphology with anterior predominance, phase lag and attenuation on stimulation favors a metabolic pattern, but it does not establish one; the ictal question is settled by a benzodiazepine trial under EEG, not by morphology
red_herrings.data_point: Generalized periodic discharges with triphasic morphology at 1.5-2 Hz
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests either that the pattern is certainly metabolic and needs no EEG follow-up, or that it is status epilepticus needing anaesthetic escalation

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: An afebrile patient with a normal temperature and only mild leukocytosis can still have spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; the paracentesis, not the temperature, decides
red_herrings.data_point: Temperature 37.0 C with WBC 12.4 x10^9/L and no abdominal pain
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests there is no infection to look for, so the precipitant is missed

sequence_constraints.reason: The hepatic and renal panel, albumin and INR decide which ASM and which dose are safe, so the laboratory work-up comes before the drug-interaction check.

eeg.impression: This is an ABNORMAL EEG due to: 1. Generalized periodic discharges with triphasic morphology at 1.5-2 Hz with anterior predominance and an anterior-to-posterior phase lag, attenuating with noxious stimulation. 2. Intermittent left temporal (T3, T5) rhythmic 3-4 Hz activity in runs of 5 to 15 seconds, distinct in morphology from the generalized pattern and without clear evolution. 3. Diffuse background slowing. No unequivocal electrographic seizure was recorded; both patterns lie on the ictal-interictal continuum and the record does not separate a metabolic from an ictal origin. Clinical correlation recommended.

labs.interpretation: Marked hyperammonemia (186 umol/L). Synthetic failure with total bilirubin 8.6 mg/dL, INR 3.2 and albumin 2.2 g/dL. Hyponatremia 128 mEq/L, hypokalemia 3.2 mEq/L and glucose 62 mg/dL. Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL with BUN 42 mg/dL. Leukocytosis 12.4 x10^9/L with anemia and thrombocytopenia. Mildly raised transaminases with an AST to ALT ratio above 2. Venous pH 7.44 with pCO2 38 mmHg (respiratory alkalosis). Magnesium and lactate normal.

metadata.clinical_pearl: Triphasic morphology does not separate hepatic encephalopathy from non-convulsive status epilepticus: reactivity, evolution and a benzodiazepine trial under EEG do. Look for the precipitant with a paracentesis even without fever. Valproate is contraindicated in liver failure and benzodiazepines accumulate in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis; levetiracetam is renally cleared and safe.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required (labs, paracentesis, CT, cEEG, drug check) + 2 recommended + 1 optional; hepatic encephalopathy precipitated by afebrile spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, with a triphasic pattern and left temporal rhythmic runs that cannot be called ictal on morphology alone; teaching is the periodic-pattern question, the paracentesis, albumin, and antiseizure medication choice in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis; LP is harmful; 2 grounded red herrings.
metadata.pitfalls: Treating the EEG pattern instead of looking for the precipitant; missing afebrile spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; valproate or maintenance benzodiazepines in cirrhosis; lumbar puncture with INR 3.2 and platelets 82; continuing propranolol and diuretics during the decompensation; titrating lactulose to ammonia levels.

metadata.teaching_points: Triphasic patterns on the ictal-interictal continuum; the ascitic polymorphonuclear threshold and albumin in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; lactulose target of 2 to 3 stools per day; antiseizure medication choice in liver failure; hypoglycemia and hyponatremia in decompensated cirrhosis.

social_history.note: Retired engineer. Married. Former heavy drinker (quit 3 years ago at cirrhosis diagnosis). Non-smoker. No illicit drugs.

patient.history_present_illness: A 74-year-old White right-handed man, a retired engineer with alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C), was admitted for confusion worsening over 3 days. His wife reports that he has been sleeping most of the day, has been increasingly disoriented, and has had 'shaking of his hands' when he holds them out. He has had three previous episodes of overt hepatic encephalopathy and takes lactulose and rifaximin; his gastroenterologist increased the lactulose 5 days ago without improvement. He stopped drinking 3 years ago at the time of diagnosis and eats poorly. He has never had a seizure. On examination he is disoriented to time and place, intermittently drowsy, and has coarse asterixis, jaundice, spider angiomata, caput medusae and moderate ascites. He was admitted to the medical ward as a further episode of hepatic encephalopathy. Neurology was called when the nurses noted intermittent rhythmic movements of the right arm, lasting a few seconds and not explained by asterixis, and the medical team is uncertain whether to treat for possible non-convulsive status epilepticus or to continue treating hepatic encephalopathy.

neurological_exam.motor: Coarse bilateral asterixis. Intermittent rhythmic movements of the right arm lasting 5 to 10 seconds, several times an hour, different in character from the asterixis. No focal weakness between episodes.
